title: Image Fundamentals
description: How computers represent and process images: pixels and channels, classic filters, preprocessing for deep learning, and vision-specific data augmentation.

lessons.title: How Computers See Images
lessons.description: Learn how an image actually becomes numbers a model can work with.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can explain how an image is represented numerically, including what pixels and channels are.

sections.title: 🖼️ An image is just a grid of numbers
sections.content: To a computer, an image is a grid of **pixels**, and each pixel is represented by one or more numbers describing its color. A grayscale image is a single 2D grid of numbers (usually 0-255, where 0 is black and 255 is white); a color image typically has three such grids stacked together — one each for red, green, and blue.

sections.title: 🎨 RGB and channels
sections.content:
A color image is usually stored with three **channels** — Red, Green, and Blue — each its own grid the same height and width as the image. Combining the three values at each pixel position produces that pixel's actual color.

```python
import numpy as np

# A tiny 2x2 RGB image: height=2, width=2, channels=3
image = np.array([
    [[255, 0, 0], [0, 255, 0]],   # red pixel, green pixel
    [[0, 0, 255], [255, 255, 255]] # blue pixel, white pixel
])
print(image.shape)  # (2, 2, 3) — height, width, channels
```

A typical photo might be 224×224×3 — 224 pixels tall, 224 pixels wide, 3 color channels — which is exactly the kind of tensor a CNN (from the deep learning course) is built to process.

sections.title: 🔢 From image to tensor
sections.content:
In a deep learning pipeline, an image is loaded and converted into a **tensor** (a multi-dimensional array) of pixel values, typically scaled to a standard range (like 0-1, dividing raw pixel values by 255) before being fed into a model — this scaling connects directly back to the feature scaling covered in the data science course, just applied to pixel intensities instead of tabular features.

```python
# Conceptual: raw pixel values (0-255) → scaled tensor (0-1)
# scaled_image = raw_image / 255.0
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Forgetting images have a channel dimension, not just height and width.** A color image tensor has 3 dimensions (height, width, channels), not 2 — an easy detail to overlook when reasoning about shapes.

**Not scaling pixel values before feeding them into a model.** Raw 0-255 values can behave poorly with typical weight initializations and learning rates — scaling to a smaller range (like 0-1) is standard practice, mirroring feature scaling from earlier courses.

**Confusing grayscale and color image shapes.** A grayscale image often has just 1 channel (or sometimes none at all, depending on the library) instead of RGB's 3 — code that assumes 3 channels can break on grayscale input.

questions.question: What does a color image's shape (height, width, channels) with channels=3 represent?
options: Three separate images stored together for backup
The three RGB color channels — Red, Green, and Blue — each contributing to every pixel's final color
The image was resized three times
Three different resolutions of the same image
questions.explanation: A standard color image stores three separate grids of values (one per Red, Green, Blue channel), all the same height and width — combining the three values at each position produces that pixel's full color.

questions.question: Why are raw pixel values (0-255) typically scaled before being fed into a deep learning model?
options: Scaling has no real effect and is purely optional
Unscaled large raw values can behave poorly with typical weight initializations and learning rates — this mirrors feature scaling from the data science course
Pixel values cannot be represented as numbers otherwise
Only grayscale images need this scaling, not color images
questions.explanation: Just like scaling numeric features in a tabular dataset, scaling pixel values (commonly to a 0-1 range) helps training behave more predictably — this is the same underlying principle as feature scaling, applied to image data.

questions.question: What's the difference between a grayscale image and a color image in terms of representation?
options: There is no real difference — both are represented identically
A grayscale image typically has a single channel of intensity values, while a color image typically has three channels (RGB)
Grayscale images cannot be represented numerically at all
Color images always have more pixels than grayscale images
questions.explanation: Grayscale images represent brightness with a single channel per pixel, while color images use three channels (Red, Green, Blue) combined to represent full color — a meaningful difference in the tensor shape a model needs to expect.

questions.question: What range are raw grayscale pixel values usually in?
options: -1 to 1
Only 0 or 1
questions.explanation: Grayscale pixel values are typically represented on a 0-255 scale, where 0 is black and 255 is white.

questions.question: What does the shape (2, 2, 3) represent for the tiny image example in the lesson?
options: 2 images of width 2 and height 3
Height 2, width 2, and 3 color channels
3 images of height and width 2
A 1-dimensional array of 12 values
questions.explanation: The shape follows the (height, width, channels) convention, so (2, 2, 3) describes a 2x2 pixel image with 3 color channels (RGB).

questions.question: Why is 224x224x3 mentioned as a typical photo tensor size?
options: It's an arbitrary number with no real significance
It matches the exact kind of tensor shape a CNN from the deep learning course is built to process
Every image must be exactly this size to be stored digitally
It only applies to grayscale images
questions.explanation: 224x224x3 is a common input size CNNs are designed around, connecting this lesson directly to the CNN architecture covered in the deep learning course.

questions.question: Why does the lesson connect pixel value scaling to the data science course's feature scaling?
options: Because pixel values and tabular features are conceptually unrelated
Because scaling pixel values to a smaller range (like 0-1) mirrors the same principle as feature scaling for tabular data
Because images cannot be scaled at all
Because feature scaling only applies to text data
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly draws this connection: scaling pixel intensities before feeding them into a model is the same underlying principle as scaling numeric features, just applied to images.

questions.question: What is a common consequence of code that assumes every image has 3 channels?
options: It always works correctly, regardless of input
It can break when given a grayscale image with only 1 channel
It automatically converts any image to color
It has no effect on any type of image
questions.explanation: Code written assuming a 3-channel (RGB) input can fail or behave unexpectedly when given a grayscale image, which often has just 1 channel instead.

lessons.title: Classic Image Processing Basics
lessons.description: Learn the hand-crafted techniques that came before deep learning, and that still power real-world vision pipelines today.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can explain what a convolution-based filter does in classic image processing and name a few common ones.

sections.title: 🔁 A familiar idea, applied by hand
sections.content: Recall convolutional filters from the deep learning course — a small grid of weights sliding across an image. Long before CNNs *learned* their filters from data, classic image processing used **hand-designed** filters for specific, well-understood effects. The underlying sliding-window computation is exactly the same idea; only where the filter's weights come from differs.

sections.title: 🌫️ Blurring and sharpening
sections.content:
A **blur filter** averages each pixel with its neighbors, smoothing out noise and fine detail. A **sharpen filter** does roughly the opposite, amplifying differences between a pixel and its neighbors to make edges and details stand out more.

```python
# Conceptual blur filter (a 3x3 averaging kernel)
# [[1/9, 1/9, 1/9],
#  [1/9, 1/9, 1/9],
#  [1/9, 1/9, 1/9]]
```

sections.title: 📐 Edge detection
sections.content:
**Edge detection** filters (like the classic Sobel filter) are hand-designed to respond strongly wherever brightness changes sharply — exactly where an object's boundary typically is.

```python
import cv2

image = cv2.imread("photo.jpg", cv2.IMREAD_GRAYSCALE)
edges = cv2.Canny(image, threshold1=100, threshold2=200)
```

This connects directly back to the CNN lessons in deep learning — a CNN's early layers often end up *learning* filters that behave remarkably similarly to these classic, hand-designed edge detectors, purely from data, without anyone telling it to.

sections.title: 🎯 Why classic techniques still matter
sections.content: Even in a deep learning-dominated field, classic image processing remains genuinely useful: it's fast, doesn't require training data or a GPU, and is often used as a preprocessing step even in modern pipelines — resizing, denoising, or normalizing an image before it ever reaches a neural network. Libraries like **OpenCV** provide efficient, well-tested implementations of these classic techniques, and remain a staple tool in real-world computer vision pipelines.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Assuming classic techniques were replaced entirely by deep learning.** They remain widely used, especially for fast preprocessing steps that don't need to be learned from data at all.

**Confusing hand-designed filters with a CNN's learned filters.** The underlying sliding-window convolution operation is identical — the key difference is that classic filters are designed by a human, while a CNN's filters are learned automatically from training data.

**Reaching for a full deep learning model when a simple classic technique would work.** For straightforward, well-understood tasks like basic edge detection or denoising, a classic filter is often faster, cheaper, and perfectly adequate.

questions.question: What is the key difference between a classic hand-designed image filter and a CNN's learned filter?
options: They use a completely different mathematical operation
A classic filter's weights are designed by a human for a specific known effect; a CNN's filter weights are learned automatically from training data
Classic filters can only be applied to grayscale images
CNN filters cannot detect edges at all
questions.explanation: Both use the same underlying sliding-window convolution operation — the real difference is where the filter's weights come from: manually designed by a person for classic filters, versus learned through training for a CNN.

questions.question: What does an edge detection filter respond strongly to?
options: Areas of completely uniform, unchanging brightness
Locations where brightness changes sharply, typically corresponding to object boundaries
The exact color of each pixel
Only the corners of an image
questions.explanation: Edge detectors are specifically designed to produce a strong response wherever there's a sharp change in brightness between neighboring pixels — exactly where an object's edge or boundary usually is in an image.

questions.question: Why do classic image processing techniques remain useful even in a deep-learning-dominated field?
options: They are actually obsolete and never used anymore
They're fast, don't require training data or a GPU, and are often used for preprocessing steps even within modern deep learning pipelines
They can only be used on very old computers
Deep learning models cannot process images that have been preprocessed with classic filters
questions.explanation: Classic techniques remain genuinely practical for cheap, fast preprocessing (like resizing, denoising, or basic edge detection) — libraries like OpenCV provide efficient implementations that are still widely used as a preprocessing step ahead of modern deep learning models.

questions.question: What does a blur filter do to an image?
options: It sharpens edges dramatically
It averages each pixel with its neighbors, smoothing out noise and fine detail
It converts the image to grayscale
It removes all color channels
questions.explanation: A blur filter smooths an image by averaging each pixel's value with its surrounding neighbors, reducing noise and fine detail.

questions.question: What is the Sobel filter an example of?
options: A blurring filter
An edge detection filter
A resizing operation
A normalization technique
questions.explanation: The Sobel filter is a classic, hand-designed edge detection filter that responds strongly to sharp brightness changes, which typically correspond to object edges.

questions.question: What connection does the lesson draw between classic edge detectors and CNNs?
options: CNNs never learn anything resembling classic edge detectors
A CNN's early layers often end up learning filters that behave remarkably similarly to classic hand-designed edge detectors, purely from data
Classic filters and CNN filters use entirely different mathematical operations
CNNs cannot detect edges under any circumstances
questions.explanation: The lesson notes that CNNs, despite learning their filters automatically, often arrive at early-layer filters that resemble classic hand-designed edge detectors like Sobel.

questions.question: What library does the lesson highlight as providing efficient implementations of classic image processing techniques?
options: PyTorch
OpenCV
TensorFlow
scikit-learn
questions.explanation: OpenCV is specifically called out as the standard library providing efficient, well-tested implementations of classic image processing techniques.

questions.question: Why does the lesson say classic image processing techniques remain useful even today?
options: They have been completely replaced by deep learning with no remaining use
They're fast, require no training data or GPU, and are often used as preprocessing steps even in modern pipelines
They can only be used on grayscale images
They require more compute than deep learning models
questions.explanation: The lesson emphasizes that classic techniques remain genuinely practical for fast, cheap preprocessing, even within otherwise deep-learning-based pipelines.

lessons.title: Image Preprocessing for Deep Learning
lessons.description: Learn the practical preparation steps that turn raw images into model-ready input.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can list the standard preprocessing steps applied to images before they're fed into a deep learning model.

sections.title: 📏 Resizing to a fixed size
sections.content:
Most CNN architectures expect a fixed input size (like 224×224), but real-world images come in all shapes and sizes. **Resizing** scales every image to the expected input dimensions before it reaches the model.

```python
import cv2

image = cv2.imread("photo.jpg")
resized = cv2.resize(image, (224, 224))
```

A common concern: naive resizing can distort an image's proportions if the original and target aspect ratios differ — techniques like **letterboxing** (padding to preserve the original aspect ratio, rather than stretching) are often used to avoid this distortion.

sections.title: 🔢 Normalization
sections.content:
Just like the feature scaling from the data science course, image pixel values are typically **normalized** — commonly scaled to 0-1, and often further standardized using a per-channel mean and standard deviation computed from a large reference dataset (like ImageNet).

```python
# Conceptual normalization matching common pretrained model expectations
# normalized = (pixel_value / 255.0 - mean) / std
```

When using a pretrained model (recall transfer learning from the deep learning course), it's essential to normalize new images using the *same* statistics the original model was trained with — a mismatch here can quietly and significantly hurt performance.

sections.title: 🎨 Color space and channel order
sections.content:
Different libraries store color images differently — OpenCV, for instance, defaults to BGR channel order rather than the more common RGB, which can cause a model's colors to look subtly (or badly) wrong if this ordering isn't accounted for.

```python
import cv2

image_bgr = cv2.imread("photo.jpg")  # OpenCV loads as BGR by default
image_rgb = cv2.cvtColor(image_bgr, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)  # convert to RGB
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Resizing without preserving aspect ratio when it matters for the task.** Naive stretching can distort objects in ways that hurt model performance, especially for tasks sensitive to exact shape.

**Normalizing with the wrong statistics for a pretrained model.** Every pretrained model expects a specific normalization scheme — using different values than what it was trained with silently degrades its performance without an obvious error.

**Mixing up BGR and RGB channel order.** This is a classic, easy-to-miss bug — colors can look subtly wrong to a model even though the image looks fine to a human eye when inspected directly.

questions.question: Why is resizing typically needed before feeding an image into a CNN?
options: Resizing has no actual purpose and is purely optional
Most CNN architectures expect a fixed input size, while real-world images come in many different original sizes
Resizing is required to convert an image into grayscale
CNNs can only process images smaller than 10x10 pixels
questions.explanation: CNN architectures are typically built around a specific expected input shape (like 224x224), so images of varying original sizes need to be resized to that consistent shape before being processed by the model.

questions.question: Why is it important to normalize a new image using the same statistics a pretrained model was originally trained with?
options: Normalization statistics have no actual effect on model performance
A pretrained model's learned weights implicitly assume a specific normalization scheme — mismatched normalization can silently and significantly hurt its performance
Pretrained models automatically detect and correct any normalization mismatch
Normalization is only relevant for models trained completely from scratch
questions.explanation: This mirrors the fine-tuning guidance from the deep learning course — a pretrained model expects input preprocessed the way its original training data was, and using different normalization values can quietly degrade performance without producing an obvious error.

questions.question: Why can mixing up BGR and RGB channel order cause problems?
options: It has no actual effect on how a model interprets an image
Different libraries (like OpenCV) may store color channels in a different order, and feeding a model channels in the wrong order can make colors look subtly or badly wrong to it
BGR and RGB always represent identical channel orderings
This issue only affects grayscale images
questions.explanation: Since a model has learned to interpret pixel values according to a specific channel order, accidentally swapping BGR and RGB (a common OpenCV pitfall) feeds it color information in the wrong order — a classic, easy-to-miss preprocessing bug.

questions.question: What technique does the lesson mention for resizing an image without distorting its proportions?
options: Cropping to a random size
Letterboxing, which pads the image to preserve the original aspect ratio
Converting to grayscale first
Doubling the image resolution
questions.explanation: Letterboxing pads an image rather than stretching it, preserving the original aspect ratio while still matching the model's expected input dimensions.

questions.question: What statistics are commonly used for standardizing pixel values, beyond simple 0-1 scaling?
options: The image's file size and format
A per-channel mean and standard deviation computed from a large reference dataset like ImageNet
The number of objects detected in the image
The camera's shutter speed
questions.explanation: Beyond basic 0-1 scaling, images are often further standardized using per-channel mean and standard deviation statistics computed from a large reference dataset such as ImageNet.

questions.question: What channel order does OpenCV use by default when loading images?
options: RGB
BGR
Grayscale only
CMYK
questions.explanation: OpenCV defaults to BGR (Blue-Green-Red) channel order rather than the more commonly expected RGB order, which can cause bugs if not accounted for.

questions.question: Why must new images be normalized using the same statistics as a pretrained model's original training data?
options: Normalization statistics have no impact on model behavior
A pretrained model's learned weights implicitly assume a specific normalization scheme, and mismatches can quietly hurt performance
Every pretrained model automatically re-normalizes new input on its own
This only matters for models trained completely from scratch
questions.explanation: This mirrors the fine-tuning guidance from the deep learning course: mismatched normalization silently degrades a pretrained model's performance without producing an obvious error.

questions.question: What is a risk of naive resizing that stretches an image to a new aspect ratio?
options: It always improves model accuracy
It can distort an image's proportions, which may hurt performance, especially for shape-sensitive tasks
It automatically applies letterboxing
It has no effect on the image at all
questions.explanation: Naive resizing that changes an image's aspect ratio can visually distort objects, which the lesson notes as a real concern letterboxing is designed to avoid.

lessons.title: Data Augmentation for Computer Vision
lessons.description: Go deeper into the specific augmentation techniques most useful for image tasks.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: By the end of this lesson, you can list common image augmentation techniques and explain how to choose ones appropriate for a given task.

sections.title: 🔁 A quick recap from deep learning
sections.content: Recall from the deep learning course: data augmentation artificially expands training data diversity by applying label-preserving transformations, directly helping fight overfitting. Computer vision is where augmentation is used most heavily and effectively, given how naturally images support these kinds of realistic transformations.

sections.title: 🖼️ Common image augmentations
sections.content:
```python
# Conceptual augmentation examples
# flipped = flip_horizontal(image)
# rotated = rotate(image, degrees=15)
# cropped = random_crop(image, size=(200, 200))
# brightened = adjust_brightness(image, factor=1.2)
# noisy = add_random_noise(image)
```

• **Flips** — horizontal flips are common and usually safe; vertical flips make sense for some subjects (aerial photos) but not others (a flipped face or car looks unnatural)
• **Rotations** — small rotations simulate camera angle variation
• **Crops** — random crops simulate different framing and partial object visibility
• **Color/brightness jitter** — simulates different lighting conditions
• **Noise** — simulates sensor noise or lower image quality

sections.title: 🎯 Choosing augmentations that make sense for the task
sections.content:
Recall from the deep learning course: an augmentation must preserve the label's correctness. This is especially task-dependent in vision:

• Flipping a photo of a cat horizontally is fine — it's still clearly a cat
• Flipping a photo of text (for an OCR task) horizontally would make it unreadable and completely wrong
• Rotating a photo of a stop sign by 180° would turn it upside down — not realistic for how stop signs actually appear in the real world

The right augmentations depend entirely on what realistic variation actually looks like for your specific task and domain.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Applying every possible augmentation without considering the task.** As the examples above show, some augmentations actively hurt certain tasks — always sanity-check whether a transformation is realistic and label-preserving for the specific problem.

**Over-augmenting to the point of distorting realistic images too heavily.** If augmented images no longer resemble what the model will see in real deployment, training on them can actually hurt rather than help.

**Applying augmentation to validation or test data.** Like other preprocessing choices, augmentation is a training-time technique — validation and test data should reflect real, unaltered examples so evaluation remains honest.

questions.question: Why might a horizontal flip be a safe augmentation for a photo of a cat, but not for a photo of text?
options: Flipping text is technically impossible to perform
A flipped cat photo still clearly shows a cat, but flipped text becomes unreadable and no longer represents valid text for an OCR task
Horizontal flips only work on animal photos
There's no actual difference in appropriateness between the two cases
questions.explanation: Whether an augmentation is appropriate depends on whether it preserves the label's correctness for the specific task — a flipped cat is still recognizably a cat, but flipped text is no longer valid, readable text, making that augmentation inappropriate for an OCR task.

questions.question: Why shouldn't data augmentation typically be applied to validation or test data?
options: Augmentation is technically impossible to apply to validation data
Validation and test data should reflect real, unaltered examples so evaluation remains an honest measure of real-world performance
Applying augmentation to test data always improves the model's reported performance
There's no real reason — augmentation should be applied everywhere equally
questions.explanation: Augmentation is specifically a training-time technique for increasing training diversity — since validation and test sets exist to honestly measure how the model performs on real, representative data, augmenting them would distort that evaluation.

questions.question: What determines whether a given augmentation technique is appropriate for a specific vision task?
options: Only how visually interesting the augmented image looks
Whether the transformation preserves the label's correctness and reflects realistic variation for that specific task and domain
Augmentations are always appropriate for every task without exception
The size of the original image file
questions.explanation: The key criterion, as with augmentation generally, is whether the transformed image remains a valid, label-preserving example that reflects realistic variation the model might actually encounter — this varies meaningfully across different vision tasks and domains.

questions.question: Why might a vertical flip make sense for aerial photos but not for a photo of a face?
options: Vertical flips are never usable for any image type
Aerial photos have no fixed 'up' orientation the way a face does, so flipping vertically still looks realistic, while a flipped face looks unnatural
Faces cannot be flipped at all technically
Vertical flips only apply to grayscale images
questions.explanation: Aerial imagery often lacks a strong sense of orientation, so a vertical flip remains realistic, whereas a flipped face looks unnatural since faces have a clear typical orientation.

questions.question: What real-world variation does color/brightness jitter augmentation aim to simulate?
options: Different camera resolutions
Different lighting conditions
Different object categories
Different image file formats
questions.explanation: Color and brightness jitter augmentations simulate the natural variation in lighting conditions that real images might be captured under.

questions.question: Why would rotating a photo of a stop sign by 180 degrees be a poor augmentation choice?
options: Rotation is technically impossible to perform on digital images
An upside-down stop sign isn't realistic for how stop signs actually appear in the real world
Stop signs cannot be photographed at any angle
180-degree rotation always improves model accuracy
questions.explanation: Since stop signs never realistically appear upside-down in the real world, this rotation would not reflect realistic variation and could actively hurt the model.

questions.question: What determines whether random cropping is an appropriate augmentation for a given task?
options: Random cropping is always appropriate for every possible task
Whether it simulates realistic differences in framing and partial object visibility relevant to that task
The color of the image being cropped
The total file size of the training dataset
questions.explanation: Like other augmentations, random cropping's appropriateness depends on whether it produces realistic variation (different framing, partial visibility) relevant to the specific task at hand.

questions.question: According to the lesson, what happens if augmented images are distorted too heavily and no longer resemble real deployment images?
options: Training on them always improves generalization regardless of distortion level
Training on over-distorted images can actually hurt rather than help performance
This has no effect on model performance either way
Over-distorted images automatically get filtered out by the model
questions.explanation: The lesson warns that over-augmenting to the point where images no longer resemble what the model will see in real deployment can hurt performance rather than help it.
